title: Not ten thousand years
hook: don't act as if you'll live ten thousand years; while you can, be good (Meditations 4.17)

segments.voice: Yesterday: take away the opinion. Your line was take away the label. When something stung, could you split the event from the label? Day five hundred fifty-four.

There's a thank-you note you've been meaning to write for about two years. An apology that's been ready in your head since last spring. A visit to an aunt who keeps saying come anytime. None of these are hard. They're just always scheduled for later, as though later were endless. Marcus Aurelius caught himself doing the same thing, and in the seventeenth entry of book four he wrote himself a reminder short enough to fit on a sticky note. Today: not ten thousand years.
screen: `THE NOTE YOU'VE MEANT TO WRITE.` → `ALWAYS SCHEDULED FOR LATER.` → `NOT TEN THOUSAND YEARS.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In George Long's 1862 translation it reads: "Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good." Three sentences. A warning, a fact, and an instruction. Second, ten thousand years. That number is the joke inside the warning. Nobody actually believes they'll live ten thousand years. But we act as if we will, putting off the good things because there's always more time. Marcus isn't accusing himself of a belief. He's accusing himself of a habit. Third, death hangs over you. Marcus doesn't say this to frighten himself. The Stoics kept death in view on purpose, as a way of sorting what matters from what doesn't. If this might be the last week, the thank-you note moves up, and the argument about the thermostat moves down. Fourth, while you can, be good. Notice he doesn't say be productive, or be famous, or finish your list. He says be good. And he puts a condition on it: while it is in your power. Not when you're less busy. Not when the kids are grown. Not when you've earned a rest. The good you've been saving isn't kept somewhere safe. It's quietly expiring. Here's the Tuesday version. Think of one good act you've been holding for later. Then ask: is later actually promised? Marcus's answer, written by an emperor who had lost several of his own children, was no.
screen: `A WARNING, A FACT, AN INSTRUCTION.` · `NOT A BELIEF, A HABIT.` · `DEATH IN VIEW, TO SORT WHAT MATTERS.` · `WHILE IT IS IN YOUR POWER.` · then, large: `BE GOOD WHILE I CAN.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one good thing you've been saving for later. A note, a call, an apology, a visit, a gift. Hold the picture of the person it's for. Then ask quietly: is later promised? Let the answer be honest. Now picture doing it today, in the smallest possible version: a two-line message, a five-minute call. Decide when. The bell holds the time.
Not ten thousand years. Marcus warns himself not to act as if life were endless: while it's in your power, be good. Today's word.
Your line: be good while I can. Do one good thing today that you've been saving for later, even in its smallest form. Day five hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often use Meditations 4.17 as a prompt to stop postponing small kindnesses, doing one saved-up good act the same day.

original.note: Greek, 'good': Marcus's instruction in 4.17 is simply to become good while you can.

trapdoor: what you thought: life is short, so enjoy it.
what it means: life is short, so do the good you've been saving, now.
what a scholar hears: keeping death in view, later called memento mori, was a Stoic discipline for sorting priorities, not for gloom.
